newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Shift in style, not policy, seen at Brazil cenbank.
newsitem.headline: Shift in style, not policy, seen at Brazil cenbank.

text.p: Thanks to the achievements of his predecessor, the man nominated to be Brazil's next central bank chief will be able to focus on what he likes best -- economic policy and boosting the country's image in world markets, bankers said.

"Gustavo Franco likes to solve economic problems and dabble in macroeconomic theory. He'll also devote more time to Brazil's place in the global market," said Paulo Guilherme Ribeiro, president of Banco Real, a leading retail bank.
The outspoken Franco, Brazil's main proponent of a strong currency and tight monetary policy, was nominated on Tuesday to replace Gustavo Loyola as central bank president.
Loyola announced he would step down soon, saying he had completed his main goal of stabilizing the nation's shaky financial system and stamping out a banking crisis.
Franco's nomination was expected to be approved by the Senate in the first two weeks of August.

"Gustavo Franco is just the opposite, and it is hard to imagine him not getting into trouble saying things he could get away with as international affairs director but not as central bank president," Bydalek said.
In fact, many bankers said off-the-cuff remarks by Franco could jolt Brazil's usually lethargic money and currency markets, which some traders said they would welcome.
The central bank has said Franco will not comment about the job until he is confirmed by the Senate.

Bankers and analysts said Franco's agenda would be simple and not very revolutionary -- maintain the current foreign exchange system in the face of increasing criticism and promote the nation's economic successes abroad.
The main difference between Franco and his predecessor is a matter of style, analysts said.
"Loyola was a poor public speaker, but a closed-mouthed, professional central banker," said Paul Bydalek, president of the rating agency Atlantic Rating.
Although Loyola dodged the limelight and was portrayed in the press as the quintessential career bureaucrat, his achievments were underrated, bankers said.

They said Loyola was forced to do most of the central bank's dirty work in overseeing the mergers and closures of dozens of banks at a time when Brazil was trying to recover from years of hyperinflation.
Precisely because Loyola was so successful, Franco would now have the freedom to devote more attention to defending the current monetary policy, bankers said.

The change of leadership at the central bank was viewed favorably in the markets, with Brazilian stocks and Brady bonds trading higher after the news. The announcement came as little surprise because Loyola had often said he would resign after he finished the restructuring of the banking sector.
"We see this as a natural progression. The evening news gave it only about five minutes," said Paulo Ferraz, president of investment bank Banco Bozano, Simonsen.
